en: The Scripture on Saving Those Who Study the Vaipulya, translated in one fascicle by the Western Jin Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The assembly was vast, consisting of sixty thousand bhikṣus, eight billion bodhisattvas, and six million upāsakas from the kingdom of Magadha.
At the time of his final nirvāṇa, in the very last year, he arrived at Rājagṛha at the commencement of the new year.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi known as "Just-as-it-is," thereby adorning this trichiliocosm: he suspended silken banners and colorful streamers, erected various pennants and canopies, scattered flowers, burned incense, and spread lotuses with hundreds of thousands of petals.

Brahma Kings by the hundreds of millions in the three thousandfold world system each went to the place where the Buddha was with countless hundreds of thousands of millions of attendants; they prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and joined their palms in self-surrender.

The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven within this great trichiliocosm—the Great Divine and Wondrous Heavenly Kings of majestic power and authority, as well as the various Dragon Kings, Ghost King Spirits, Asura Kings, Garuḍa Kings, Kiṃnara Kings, and Mahoraga Kings—each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of attendants, went to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined, took refuge in him.

From each of the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of divine and peerless excellence, of lofty and eminent character, came to the place where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined, took refuge in him.

All those who had gathered pervaded this trichiliocosm at that moment, reaching as far as the thirty-two heavens of the upper realms; there was no empty space—so dense that a staff could not be inserted between them and even a needle could not pass through—leaving nothing but a continuous mass.
The Great Devas of the Infinite Heavens, dragons, ghosts, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas each stood in their respective places, gazing upon the venerable countenance of the Buddha.
Their bodies were each distinct, yet their minds were one; having relinquished causal conditions, they returned to the Buddha with equanimity.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi with serene composure and observed the assembled multitude three times.
Having observed this three times, he performed the lion’s stretch three times.
Having stretched three times, he extended his tongue three times.
Having extended his tongue three times, he covered the trichiliocosm with it three times, such that there was nowhere it did not pervade; its brilliant radiance shone throughout the ten directions.
Thereupon, the Great Sage withdrew his tongue and again surveyed all those who had gathered for the assembly.
All those present rose from their seats, bowed their heads in prostration, and took refuge in the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Ajita! You should know and be aware that before long, the Perfectly Awakened One shall enter parinirvāṇa."
If you have anything you wish to ask, now is the time; you should inquire and request instruction.
Should there be any lingering doubts or knots of uncertainty, or any matters for which your mind finds no resolution, come before the Tathāgata to question him. Do not later regret it by saying:
"When I was face-to-face with the Great Sage, why did I not resolve these matters?"
Maitreya Bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you know the proper time; you have attained clarity through the six supernormal powers and the various perfections (pāramitās), and there is nothing you do not proclaim or resolve regarding all doubts.”
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
It is timely and appropriate that you proclaim the Way of the Sūtras, so that these eyes of the Dharma may endure forever.
Thereupon, the Great and Wondrous Heavenly King, surrounded by a retinue of eight billion devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Bowing my head at your feet and joining my palms in self-refuge, I came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
This present sutra is titled 'Saving All Vaipulya Students,' and it is that which was expounded by the Buddhas of the past—Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

Today, Great Sage, you should deign to show compassion and once again expound upon the meaning of the teachings, out of great pity and for the sake of great peace and security, so that the Dharma-instructions of the Tathāgata may endure for a long time.
At that time, the Buddha remained silent, thereby granting his assent to what the Great and Wondrous Heavenly King had requested.
Seeing that the Buddha had granted his assent by remaining silent, the Heavenly King withdrew and stood to one side.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Ajita, you should know that among all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, there were none who did not expound this essential sūtra that delivers through the Vaipulya;
likewise, the Tathāgatas, Arhats of the future and present in the worlds of the ten directions all preach it as well."
If one does not proclaim this, they slander the Buddha, contravene the sūtras, and disparage the assembly of noble ones. Why is this so?
If one speaks of this sūtra with the notion that it is of no benefit, or claims it is incomplete, they are slandering the Buddha, violating and losing the scriptures, and reviling the noble assembly.
Those who disparage the Triple Gem will inevitably fall into hell. Therefore, Maitreya,

if sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle have mastered and thoroughly understood all the various scriptures and diverse teachings of others, they may then analyze and expound upon the meanings of these various scriptures.
If you wish to be fully equipped and not deficient in words and letters, you should follow the authentic scriptures and teachings without diminishing yourself.
Furthermore, O compassionate Maitreya!
You should single-mindedly and diligently contemplate this gate, and thereafter protect and uphold the True Dharma in the final age.
Maitreya replied:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
It is truly as the holy teaching declares; I shall transmit the divine intent and dare not disobey your command.”
The Buddha again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"From the day the Tathāgata, the Arhat, attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path and became the Most Perfectly Awakened One, until the night he entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder—during all that time, did the Tathāgata, the Arhat, ever have any deficiency or flaw, or any error of mind or forgetfulness?"
"Is it not a fault to proclaim evil thoughts?
Maitreya replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
He further addressed Ajita:

"From the night the Tathāgata attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the day of his parinirvāṇa, everything he has preached is true and sincere; it accords with the proper time and is appropriate to the occasion, being entirely free from falsehood."
The Buddha said:

"There may be foolish people who do not distinguish the Tathāgata’s skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and fail to perceive his words of true and authentic reality; instead, they spread mad talk, speaking according to their own whims:
'This matter accords with the Dharma, while this meaning does not accord.'"
"By drawing such analogies, they slander the Right Path.
To slander the sutras is to slander the Buddha; I declare that such a faction will surely fall into hell.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

"In the future final age, during the fifty remaining years of the five turbidities, there shall be four classes of followers—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—who resolve to study as bodhisattvas and yearn for their original vows; though their outward inclinations differ from those of other schools, they shall serve and honor the Tathāgata."
Having seen the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya, they leave the household life to become śramaṇas, yet they show only humble respect toward their own lineage.

Their aspirations are directed solely toward gain and offerings; they ruin their lineage, covetously envy their households, and bring disorder to their domestic affairs. Their countenances lack a healthy complexion, their wills are petty, and by nature they lack understanding. They cannot be broad-minded or serene, nor do they destroy their passions; they are restless in their constant pursuit of much.

They remain far removed from all practices of the Dharma-gates and from samādhi and right concentration, dwelling always in flattery, with minds that differ from one another and words and deeds that do not accord.
Coveting their lineage, they rely on those who possess power; yet when they see those of clear wisdom who thoroughly understand the treasury of the Dharma, they call them ignorant.
Having no knowledge themselves, they boast of their own wisdom;
lacking intelligence themselves, they praise themselves as clever and wise.

Relying on the Buddha-way to establish their resolve, they maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion; furthermore, they do not forget or abandon skillful means.
It is solely by relying on the power of the Buddha that they do not transgress what has been taught, but instead place their faith and delight within that learning.
Or again, they may say:
"If there are sutra scrolls that speak of the matters of the śrāvakas, a bodhisattva-practitioner should not study them, nor should they listen to them.
These are not our dharma, nor are they the principles of our path; they are the practices of the śrāvakas. Those who cultivate the bodhisattva path must be careful not to study them."
“The Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas is also like this; you must be careful not to listen to it.
The Buddha said to Ajita:

“The Buddha, for the sake of those who have faith and joy, transforms and enlightens the various devas, preaching the Dharma according to the occasion. He teaches the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, gandharvas, humans, and non-humans, preaching the Dharma to transform and enlighten them according to their original conduct and what their aspirations require for liberation.”

They reach everywhere throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, guiding and benefiting sentient beings according to their respective past practices; they deliver and benefit sentient beings as is appropriate for each.
By means of this resolve, they proclaim the Way of the Sutras, delivering and liberating all so that everyone may attain the Path.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"At that time, among the bodhisattvas in training, their minds will harbor fetters; they will be stubborn and difficult to transform among the assembly of bodhisattvas, being corrupt, evil, and violent, given to false speech and double-tonguedness, with little learning and meager wisdom."
They propagate the Buddha-way by dividing it into two parts, saying:
"If you wish to be a bodhisattva, you should study this dharma and not study that.
Holding such a mind, they slander the Buddha, disparage the sutras, and cause strife among the assembly of sages.

When their lives end and their bodies disperse, they shall fall into hell, where they will be seen being boiled; they shall endure suffering for countless kalpas, yet their transgressions will still not be exhausted.

Upon emerging from hell, they shall again be reborn into the doors of poverty and destitution, experiencing the calamities and afflictions of manifold hardships; only after traveling an exceedingly distant and immeasurable distance shall they finally receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Although he has received the prediction of enlightenment, he shall only become a Buddha in an age of the five turbidities;
this is just as I myself originally encountered hardships for a vast and incalculable number of kalpas before attaining supreme perfect enlightenment in an age of the five turbidities.
If one hears these words and believes them, accepts them, and with deep faith reflects upon and follows their teaching, one shall likewise fall into the evil destinies.
This is because, by trusting in evil friends, one encounters such calamity.
The Buddha told Ajita:

"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vigatamala-jvala-siddhārtha-yaśas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world for eighty koṭis of years, proclaiming the Way of the Sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Śuddhajīva who served as the presiding lecturer for the Dharma.

He proclaimed various teachings with gentle and supple speech; his eloquence was most authentic, and he inspired and encouraged countless people, widely propagating the equal teaching to the great joy of many.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vimalasiddhayaśas entrusted the bhikṣu Śuddhajīva with the task of protecting the True Dharma during the final age; having thus entrusted him, he then entered parinirvāṇa.
"After the Tathāgata, the Truly Perfected One, has entered parinirvāṇa, that bhikṣu shall uphold the Dharma-piṭaka for a hundred million years and proclaim the Buddha's teachings.

Thereby, he will universally enter the essentials of the Vaipulya sūtras to rescue all beings, disseminating the transformative influence of the Way to initiate all things; he shall analyze and distinguish according to what each sentient being’s fundamental mind desires and ought to understand."

He traveled back and forth through eighty thousand cities and towns, observing the original vows and initial aspirations of sentient beings, causing them to attain full satisfaction and removing the hardships of their hunger and emptiness.
"In that world at that time, there was a great royal city named Bhadra.
Eight billion people lived within it; he also observed their roots and conditions and preached the Dharma for them."

At that time, eight billion households within the city joyfully accepted the teaching; one hundred million households were inspired to resolve upon the path of a bodhisattva, while seven hundred and ninety million established themselves in the vehicle of the śrāvaka.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu Śuddhājīva and ten thousand bodhisattvas went together with one mind to the place where the Way was practiced.
Not long after they had departed, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmakāra who arrived from afar, traveling about from other regions.
In the city of Renxian (Bhadra), he upheld more than a thousand scrolls of Vaipulya sutras; having attained the four dhyānas, he considered himself far advanced.
The bhikṣu Jingming (Viśuddhājīva) studied fourteen hundred million scrolls of Vaipulya sutras, as well as six million scrolls of other scriptures.

At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmabhāṇaka resided in the city of Bhadra and preached only a single category of Dharma teaching; he did not know how to observe their fundamental conduct according to the occasion to expound the sutras and dharmas.

He was unable to awaken to or penetrate the various dharma-realms, but specialized in converting others through the dharma of emptiness alone, saying that all dharmas are empty and utterly non-existent, and in whatever he preached, he discussed only the dharma of emptiness.
They claim there is neither sin nor merit and hold all conditioned practices in contempt; furthermore, they assert of themselves:
"Everything I have now spoken is the teaching of the Buddha.
As for what the bhikṣus of pure livelihood may expound, it is merely a reliance on trivialities; their disposition is not pure, and they are defiled and turbid."
Whoever originally gave that bhikṣu the name "Pure Livelihood" was truly mistaken.
Why is this? Because he accepted various flowers, and having accepted them, he consumed them.
They also receive various kinds of incense and mixed ointments, which they consume as food.
Those students are ignorant and deluded, possessing no knowledge.
As for me, I have practiced since long ago and have cultivated the holy life for a great length of time.
"He has only recently begun his studies and has just received these precepts; it has not been long since he first came here, so do not place trust in him.
Furthermore, while that bhikṣu was negligent and self-indulgent, the people paid him unwarranted respect, whereas they devoted their whole hearts with joy to the bhikṣu of pure livelihood.
In that Dharma, such bhikṣus slander and defame others, proclaiming their evil deeds; consequently, people do not believe them nor follow their teachings.
Because those bhikṣus harbor poisonous hearts and calumniate the wise, after their lives end they fall into hell for eighty kalpas.
Because they calumniate the Buddha and disparage the True Dharma, after seventy kalpas in hell, they further spend sixty kalpas in a state of delusion and loss of will.
Having completed this number of eons, he finally reached the presence of the Tathāgata Original Vow of Arousing the Mind for the Path, Fragrant Jewel Radiance Buddha.
That Buddha preached for him, further expounding the meaning of the Dharma and exhorting him to arouse the mind for the path.

He fell among the animals for nine million lifetimes; subsequently, he was born as a human being for six million lifetimes, constantly encountering poverty and misfortune, and in every place where he was born, he was always mute and tongueless.

Thereafter, he beheld sixty-three *koṭis* of Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, in the world; in the presence of these Buddhas, he constantly served as a Dharma-preacher. In every birth throughout his successive lives, he universally attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), was always seen and instructed by the Buddhas, fully understood all dharmas, and expounded their pure meaning.
The Buddha told Ajita:
"If you wish to know whether the bhikṣu of pure livelihood at that time was anyone other than myself,
do not hold such a view."
Why is this so? Because he is Amitābha Buddha.
That Dharma bhikṣu was none other than my own self; such were the experiences I underwent in that world.
The Buddha told Ajita:
"The various matters and all dharmas are difficult to comprehend, exceedingly difficult to comprehend; their meaning is subtle in this way.
For this reason, I have attained perfect enlightenment within the world of the five turbidities."
The Buddha said to Ajita:
"If there is a bodhisattva who preaches two kinds of Dharma, by virtue of this, they shall attain the Way of the Buddha within the world of the five turbidities."

Furthermore, in that buddha-field there will be many māras who repeatedly incite chaos; when he attains the Way of the Buddha, they will likewise disturb and disrupt him even as he proclaims the Dharma of the sutras.
At that time, the entire assembly gathered there was filled with distress, tears streaming down their faces, each saying to themselves:
“May practitioners not be forced to proclaim these two kinds of teachings or lecture upon the meaning of the sutras!”

Do not allow those who are biased, ignorant, unrestrained, and self-righteous to despise fellow bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma; do not speak to the bhikṣus and the lay followers in a way that discriminates against them by declaring their teachings to be non-Dharma.
At that time, there were one hundred bodhisattvas in the assembly who immediately rose from their seats, withdrew to sit on the ground, and wept with sobs and tears.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the beginning and end of these bodhisattvas' thoughts, again asked:
"O sons of good family!
"For what reason are you sitting on the ground, sighing and weeping?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, World-Honored One!"
"Each of you must examine yourselves and recognize these transgressions.
The Buddha said, "It is even so, noble sons; this is what you should observe and contemplate."
During the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was a bodhisattva named Jñānakośa who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, became a master of the Dharma.

Various worthy ones sought out his flaws and omissions; from that time forward, he has never again encountered the Buddhas, has not recognized the mind of the Way, has not attained dhāraṇī, and has not reached samādhi.
"Sons of good family, in previous lives you also joined me in giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Furthermore, sons of good family,
at the end of this *piṭa*-kalpa there will be a Buddha named Luyou."

Only in that world shall you be able to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); thereafter, after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a most perfectly awakened one (samyaksaṃbuddha).
Therefore, son of good family!
When bodhisattvas encounter one another, they must not give rise to divergent thoughts or seek out each other's faults.
If you see a bodhisattva, you should reflect to yourself:
"Now I behold the Buddhist temple and see the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment;
the Buddha stands before me. O son of good family!
If there should be a bodhisattva who, seeing another bodhisattva, gives rise to a divergent thought and views them as not being the Buddha, he thereby brings about his own ruin.
For this reason, do not harbor anger or resentment.

To regard one who has first resolved to attain the Bodhicitta as being no different from a Buddha is to immediately commit an offense against the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the countless and limitless worlds existing in the present.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Now the Buddha foresees that in the final fifty years of the future degenerate age, there will be those who attain dhāraṇī or reach samādhi; all of this is brought about by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
Therefore, son of good family!
If one slanders a Dharma teacher or seeks out their faults, they are slandering the Tathāgata.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if there is one who understands what is appropriate for the occasion and preaches the essentials of the Dharma according to the fundamental inclinations and conduct of sentient beings, [they are acting as my representative].
If, within a great assembly, there is a bodhisattva who, for even the duration of a single thought-moment of resolve, has their hair stand on end;
or who, upon hearing a sutra but once, immediately recites it from memory—then one should know that such a person is sustained by the sacred intent of the Tathāgata.
"In that world at that time, there will be foolish men who lack the bodhisattva practice yet claim to be bodhisattvas.

Among the bodhisattvas, they will be fierce, stubborn, and self-opinionated; they will analyze the scriptures, hide their own shortcomings, and claim to have attained realization alone, thereby establishing two distinct paths."
He constantly says to himself:
"What does this person know?
What does this person understand?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"The teachings I have now proclaimed in verse, as well as when I was practicing the path of a Buddha, I gave away my head, eyes, limbs, flesh, wife, children, kingdom, and cities; the Buddha remembers them all. It was for the sake of a single verse that I gave away the whole world."

"These people, deluded and ignorant, seek only profit and sustenance; they do not go to pay respect to the Buddha or those who proclaim the Way and its teachings. They do not follow the Buddha’s instructions and violate the precepts of the Path.
The Buddha said, "Ajita!"
One should uphold this Dharma with clarity and harmony, not through contention. "Ajita!
Observe how the beings of this faction habitually follow after their own defects and give rise to anger; it is because they do not contemplate maturely nor understand the meaning."
When I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment as I have practiced, and am proclaiming the Buddha-wisdom by preaching the Dharma, I shall then say:
"Do not propagate this teaching for the sake of profit and offerings in that world at that time."
That Dharma-bhikṣu expounded more than a thousand fascicles of Vaipulya sutras and gave rise to the four dhyānas; it was because of this that he encountered such hardship.
How much more so for one who speaks falsely, deviates from the principles of meaning, and does not accord with the Way and its teachings?

"If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the Vaipulya teachings and proclaims the Vaipulya treasury, thereby giving rise to the mind of enlightenment, yet instead conceives a mind to slander that Dharma Master, he is then slandering the sūtras of all Buddhas; he harbors extreme arrogance and seeks out their flaws."
The Buddha does not say that such people will reach the ultimate end and exhaust the source of birth and death; rather, those of this kind will inevitably fall into hell.
Why is this? If there are those who seek out the faults of the Dharma Master, they are thereby showing contempt for the Buddha and harboring weariness toward the sutras and the Dharma.
To disparage the Dharma Master is to show no reverence for the Buddha.
If one does not wish to behold the Dharma Master, that person does not wish to see the Buddha;
if one reviles the Dharma Master, one reviles all Buddhas.

If one gives rise to a harmful mind and thinks ill of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment], then from that moment of generating such a harmful intent, they shall lose their resolve for the Way for countless and various kalpas.
Because they looked upon the bodhisattva with an evil eye, they shall be born blind for as many successive lifetimes as the number of times they did so.
Because they slandered the Dharma-preacher with their mouths, uttering insults based on his original name, they shall remain mute and tongueless for as many kalpas as the number of such instances.
The Buddha told Ajita:
"The Buddha observes universally and sees that there is no other cause by which bodhisattvas quickly fall into the evil destinies, except for harboring an evil mind toward other bodhisattvas."
"Because they conceive of a self, a person, and a human being, and greedily dwell upon their seeking for the Dharma, they fall into the evil destinies.
The Buddha said, "Ajita!"

The Tathāgata does not consider one who propagates scriptures that follow inverted teachings, whose thoughts dwell on birth and death with self-indulgence and negligence, and who abides in the notions of a self and persons while practicing various dharmas, to be a bodhisattva.
For this reason, one falls into hell.
Therefore, Ajita!
When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they are able to achieve the Buddha-wisdom of supreme, true, and correct enlightenment.
"Or there may be some foolish person who publicly declares:
'A bodhisattva should study only the Prajñāpāramitā; other sūtras are not pāramitās,' and thus speaks disparagingly of them."
"Ajita, what do you think?
Was the king of old lacking in wisdom for giving his head as an offering to others?
Maitreya replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The six pāramitās that the Buddha originally cultivated were indeed practiced with utmost sincerity and truthfulness."
“Is it by not practicing these that one attains the Buddha-way? Maitreya replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ajita:

“In your past lives, you fully practiced the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla), and the perfection of patience (kṣānti) for sixty kalpas; the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) that you cultivated were likewise each for sixty kalpas.”
Yet those who are foolish and dull-witted each speak thus:
"One should attain the path of Buddhahood by practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* through a single practice alone.
Following such inversions, they have no aspiration or joy for the true path.
Although such people have words on their lips, their conduct is not pure;
they speak empty words that contradict the teachings and constantly act with attachment;
they long for emptiness yet refuse to practice it.

He merely speaks with his mouth as if it were the foremost thing; though he travels far, he harbors greed, envy, and jealousy, and places his respect upon lineage, kin, and acquaintances. I would rather give my head to others than accept the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
These people, being greedily attached to clothing, food, and material gain, enter the homes of others and say these words:
"The practice of the Way is like this;
for one who practices in this way, the principle is such, and there is no other meaning."
"Many Dharma masters do not understand this teaching; for the sake of gain and offerings, they frequently give rise to harmful intentions and harbor ill will toward other Dharma masters.
The Buddha said, "Ajita!"

The Buddha does not consider those who are greedy for their own lives—fools devoid of the Way—to be practitioners of the Way; even if such persons were to practice for a hundred kalpas, they would not attain the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (anulomikī-kṣānti), let alone achieve the ultimate state of Buddhahood.
The Buddha said:

“Ajita! Those who practice flattery and deceit are stingy, greedy, and envious; they do not practice reverence and lack wise insight. Clutching to their own lineage with jealousy, they perform two kinds of practices while seeking the Way.”
These foolish people, claiming for themselves that their own wisdom is clear and superior to the Buddha’s insight,
do so because they recklessly declare:
"The words with which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma are not like this."
"This is the business of the śrāvakas; the Buddha does not preach the Dharma for śrāvakas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) fundamentally one and not of dual practice?"
Subhūti replied, "So it is, O God among Gods!
He asked again:
“Subhūti, does the bodhisattva’s practice consist in relinquishing all conceptualizations and being without attachment?
“Indeed it does, World-Honored One.”
He asked again:
“Subhūti! Does the bodhisattva’s practice consist in abandoning all restlessness and remaining without negligence?”
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“How could one see a student who does not cultivate himself and knows no sense of shame?”
"To desire the reward of merit and yet encounter poverty and distress;
to seek the favor of powerful families and hope for their assistance—how exceedingly foolish this is!
The Buddha spoke again to Ajita:
“Even if a bodhisattva hears it said that all dharmas are the dharmas of śrāvakas, they should not be terrified.
Even if they hear that all dharmas are the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, or that all dharmas are the dharmas of the Buddha, they should not be terrified.”
Do not harbor expectations or cling to anything.
All dharmas are the dharmas of ordinary beings; all dharmas are the dharmas of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). Even if you hear these words, you should not be terrified.
All dharmas are the dharmas of anger; all dharmas are the dharmas of freedom from resentment. Even if you hear these words, you should not be terrified.

Whether there is something received or nothing received; whether there is action or non-action; concealment or non-concealment; purity or impurity; having a mind or being mindless; having mindfulness or being without mindfulness; having fault or being without fault; having merit or being without merit; having retribution or being without retribution; having peace or being without peace; having liberation or being without liberation; diligence or indolence; having practice or being without practice; cultivating the dharmas of the noble ones or not cultivating the dharmas of the noble ones; tranquility or lack of tranquility; receiving or not receiving; sincerity or falsehood; following right mindfulness or not following right mindfulness; abiding or not abiding—in all these phenomena, he is forever without fear.

"When the Buddha was originally practicing his studies, beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained realization of all dharmas and achieved supreme perfect enlightenment. He thoroughly understood the realms of all sentient beings, perceiving them all without inversion; he clearly comprehended all dharmas as being spontaneously so, non-attached, and without locus."
Therefore, for the sake of worldly beings, I have analytically explained that this Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, does not designate himself as any phenomena, nor does he engage in any dispute.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva attains the infinite radiance of the holy light and the splendor of the Dharma; he brings forth the dhāraṇīs and proclaims the seals of the Dharma (dharmamudrā), and for the sake of all phenomena, he remains without any sense of superiority or inferiority.
The Buddha said to Ajita:
"For the sake of the Dharma, the Buddha proclaims the Way of the sutras throughout the four quarters.
Sentient beings each think:"
"The Tathāgata has expounded the meaning of the sūtras for me through such analogies," [he thought].
Thus he proceeded as far as the twenty-fourth heaven, the Akaniṣṭha;
thereafter, he further converted and transformed a second region, reaching as far as the twenty-fourth heaven.
The trichiliocosm is also like this; all sentient beings think:
"The Tathāgata has been born here to turn the wheel of Dharma and preach the sutras and teachings."
"In this manner, through countless skillful means, I shall go to infinite and boundless worlds to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
The Buddha-works I perform throughout my travels during the morning will be immeasurable;
it shall be the same at midday and in the late afternoon."
The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is eternally thus and never ceases; his vision is without obstruction, universally beholding the realms of all sentient beings.
All Buddha-lands are likewise infinite, and the domains of the various Buddhas are also such.
“Bodhisattvas should all train in this meaning: while dwelling in the realm of conceptual constructions regarding all phenomena, they should bring beings to spiritual maturity.
If one dwells with expectations toward the Buddhas, one is already dwelling in the slander of the Buddhas;
and if one dwells in the slander of the Buddhas, one dwells in falling into perilous paths.”
Those who fall onto perilous paths will fall into the evil realms; those who dwell in the evil realms will dwell in places of contention regarding all dharmas.
Therefore, Ajita, you should protect the Tathāgata’s skillful means;
it is the Buddha himself who speaks this Dharma according to the appropriate time.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas Saṃbhavagati, Amoghadarśin, Ekavyūhacitta, Suparijñātavākcitta, Vigarhitavyūha, Priyarāja, Vigataroṣaloma-harṣa-aviṣādavikrama, Aparimitabuddhakṣetracittapraṇidhāna, Avalokiteśvara, Gandhahastin, Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Anikṣiptadhura, Śatapuṇyakoṭi-samavasaraṇa, Ojastejasvaranirghoṣa, Apratihatacittasarvajñatāpraṇidhāna, Yaśakīrtidhvaja, Arthasamdhicintin, Abhedyabuddhaviṣayacaryā, Candrottaptatejorāja, and Mahāviṣayavyūha.
Mañjuśrī addressed these twenty bodhisattvas and further said to the Buddha: “So it is, so it is!
World-Honored One!”
It is exactly as the holy teaching says.

I have traveled to the east, passing through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of sixty Ganges Rivers, where I paid homage to the World-Honored Ones and heard the Dharma they preached, just as I do today;
it was likewise so in the Buddha-fields of the west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Having traveled for seven days, they proceeded further ahead, yet saw no other Buddhas.
They soon returned and came to this land to prostrate themselves and listen to the sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
“Virtuous one, observe this immeasurable holy wisdom of the Tathāgata.
If the realm of these Buddhas is thus inconceivable and so majestically sublime;
if that which the Tathāgata enters is peerless and without equal, encompassing all things without exception.”
There may be some who are foolish and ignorant of the principles of meaning, who rashly say to themselves:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is that which the Tathāgata has practiced; it is the boundless cultivation and teaching of all Tathāgatas, whereas all other sūtras are not the words of the Buddha."
“Mañjuśrī! The practice of a bodhisattva-practitioner is a practice free from conjunction; this is the correct and true practice of a bodhisattva.

Practice that is peerless is the practice of a bodhisattva; practice that is without reception is the practice of a bodhisattva; practice that is without attachment, nor even non-attachment, is the practice of a bodhisattva.”
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!
The conduct of a bodhisattva is free from contempt; I have explained it by making distinctions according to the occasion.
All dharmas are difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!

All you worthy ones should cultivate the practice of tranquility and non-negligence, follow the steadfast conduct of the true sages, and always maintain a mind of loving-kindness, refraining from anger or harm.
Those who dwell in the cultivation of the equal practice of all dharmas follow the Buddha's teaching.
For countless eons, the Buddha has followed and practiced this path, proclaiming it through skillful means.
There will be ignorant people, each harboring divergent views, who fall into great hardship and shall give rise to ridicule and slander, reviling the Way of the sutras, saying:
"This was not proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
Those who disparage the Dharma do not perceive even the slightest fault, remaining seated without guarding their speech.
Or they may think to themselves:
"This matter is excellent," or "It is not excellent."
Thus, they slander the Dharma.
By slandering the Dharma, they slander the Buddha;
having slandered the Buddha, they revile the Sangha of the noble ones.
"To speak with a biased mouth, saying:
'This matter is appropriate; this matter is inappropriate'—one who speaks thus slanders the Dharma."
"To preach this matter for the sake of bodhisattvas, or to expound such a teaching for the sake of śrāvakas"—
to speak these words is to slander the Dharma.
"To say falsely, 'Bodhisattvas should study this dharma, they should abandon that dharma,
and they should not practice or study this,' is to slander the Dharma."

"To falsely criticize others by saying, 'So-and-so possesses eloquence, while so-and-so lacks it; so-and-so is naturally clever and facile, while so-and-so is naturally dull and slow,' and to speak of the sutras in such a manner, constitutes slandering the Dharma."
"If one were to declare:
'When encountering the era of a Buddha, one may attain dhāraṇī;
when not encountering the era of a Buddha, one cannot attain dhāraṇī.'"
"To say, 'Although one has attained dhāraṇī through practice, the dhāraṇī thus attained is not necessarily pure'—
to speak in this way is to slander the Dharma."
"To seek out the faults of a Dharma teacher, observing deficiencies in their discipline or conduct, is to slander the Dharma.
To lack faith in the complete integrity of a Dharma teacher’s practice—even if that teacher does not conform to formal decorum—is to slander the Dharma."
"To proclaim the negligent conduct of Dharma masters, to act according to one's own whims without single-mindedness, and to slander the Dharma;
to lack ritual propriety, to deviate from the scriptures and violate the rules, to fail to uphold the precepts, and to be restless and turbulent—these constitute slandering the Dharma."
"To proclaim doctrines and principles whose illumination is not extensive, yet to lecture on them recklessly, is to slander the Dharma.
To have speech that is unclear and eloquence that is not fluent, yet to desire to transmit the Way and its teachings, is to slander the Dharma."

"I have not been diligent in my studies; what I know is extremely meager and my understanding is neither broad nor profound. Yet I wish to proclaim the Way and its teachings—this would be slandering the Dharma.
He thought to himself:
"I do not know my limits, nor do I understand how to act according to the occasion. I must provide instruction and transformation, leading them to realize the ultimate meaning."
"To slander the Dharma.
To give rise to conceptual thoughts and fail to protect the Buddha’s teachings, harboring harmful intent, is to slander the Dharma.
Each person obtains a single scroll of textual scripture and instruction, yet each contends over the meaning of what they have studied, losing the true meaning; this is to slander the Dharma."
"Each reciting a single verse, they dispute its meaning and principles, asserting their own views as right and others as wrong, thereby slandering the Dharma.
They say, 'So-and-so possesses faith and joy, while so-and-so is not devoted to the Path; so-and-so shall attain liberation, while so-and-so shall not.'"
"This constitutes slandering the Dharma.

'If, when the Dharma is being expounded, one's words differ from those of others and they contradict the underlying principles, claiming that it is not what was taught by such-and-such a person, and thus comes to disrupt the assembly with idle chatter and talk of worldly affairs—this constitutes slandering the Dharma.'"
"To say, 'This person should practice this; that person should not practice this; such a thing is compliant;
such a thing is non-compliant,' is to slander the Dharma.
To say, 'Such a person acts according to the occasion; such a person does not know the occasion'—"
"To deviate from the principles of meaning and fail to follow the precepts of the Way is to slander the Dharma.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"Whatever the assembly of śrāvakas may harbor within them and explain through their analytical discourse, and whatever the bodhisattvas, with their intelligence and eloquence, may proclaim—all of this is sustained by the majestic spiritual power and sacred intent of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata’s teaching follows what is appropriate for the time; such is his vow."

These foolish people think only of disparagement; they seek out faults, do not follow the Buddha’s teachings, and instead revile the Tathāgata and the Dharma masters whom they should honor. All such individuals are utterly deluded by Māra.
Because they harbor such intentions for the sake of seeking gain and offerings, they shall fall into the evil destinies.

While they protect the virtuous and close ties upon which their household life depends, they conversely fail to guard themselves while dwelling within the teaching of the Tathāgata; they rely instead on those of noble power and high status—kings, elders, and brahmins.
If there should be someone who questions the meaning and recites the principles of the doctrine, everyone would together exclaim in praise:
"Excellent is this teaching!
What you know is admirable and delightful, just as the Buddha has taught."
"What has been proclaimed is extremely reasonable.
They all unanimously encouraged and assisted one another; because of this encouragement and assistance, they fell into the dharma of slander.
Moving together as a single faction in their comings and goings, they then perished and all fell into the evil realms.
The Buddha again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“If there is a bodhisattva who clings to and is attached to various conditioned phenomena, I do not call such a person a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
“Ajita! As for those who rely on noble lineage and hold positions of high status, the Buddha does not say that this constitutes purity.
If there are those who proclaim the meanings of two classes of sutras while their words and deeds differ, the Buddha does not say they shall attain liberation; they will surely fall into hell.”

Even if someone were to specialize in explaining a single category, claiming that its meaning and intent could not be surpassed, the Buddha would not say that such a person has transcended the hardships and afflictions of the evil realms.
"One who uses many words and delights in the clamor of crowds—such a person, the Buddha says, does not correspond to pure conduct.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"The Dharma-gates proclaimed by the Buddha to rectify all inversions are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; whether they concern advancing or retreating, they are likewise so."
The number of those who delight in and cling to emptiness regarding the Dharma-gates I have proclaimed is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

likewise, the limit of those for whom I have proclaimed the teachings of the Dharma-gates by reckoning them as having a self due to their various false imaginings is also as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Sentient beings are likewise like karma without conceptualization and the source of all conceptualization, and like karma without aspiration and the root of all aspirations; for them, he preaches Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

There are those who hold that there is a person and those who hold that there is no person; those who hold that there is a life-principle and those who hold that there is none; those who hold that there is a lifespan and those who hold that there is none; those who hold that there is desire and those who hold that there is none; those who hold that there is greed and those who hold that there is none; those who hold that there is the conditioned and those who hold that there is the unconditioned. Some people diligently follow the calculation of permanence, while others do not so diligently but merely contemplate annihilation. Some find pleasure in following worldly conventions, while others seek to transcend the world. Some enter through the gate of greed, some through the gate of hatred, and some through the gate of delusion. The Tathāgata causes all these various gates to be removed, and for this reason, he expounds the Dharma-gate.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"If there is one who practices the appropriateness of equanimity and is forever without attachment, all such persons accord with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā."

"If there are those who preach with various differing understandings, whose minds dwell on what they have seen and heard, and who expound that which does not accord with wisdom, they slander the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
These types of people, having been led astray by evil friends and received false teachings, are able to give rise to such slander.
By what means can they reproach themselves in the present life so as to eliminate their transgressions?
The World-Honored One then addressed Mañjuśrī:

"Suppose this person, for a period of seven years, were to repent and reproach themselves three times each day and night; only then would the sin of slander they have committed be eliminated and subtly digested."
"Furthermore, after practicing for fifteen more kalpas, one shall then attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

If a bodhisattva practices the essentials of this sutra but cannot understand them clearly and yet recklessly proclaims them, they will find it extremely difficult to resolve those matters and attain liberation;
for the dharma of written words disperses the meaning and fails to convey it fully.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva must first study with thorough and careful attention before being able to proclaim [the Dharma]; one who studies in this way does not harm themselves.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva thoroughly understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). What are these four?

First, to have a mind of equanimity that takes pity on sentient beings; second, to understand all dharmas with equanimity and without partiality; third, to be equanimous regarding the meaning of the Path and not to rely on either the heterodox or the orthodox; fourth, to speak with impartiality and not harbor deluded thoughts. These are the four.
If one does not understand these four equalities and speaks recklessly, one will bring harm upon oneself.
"If sons of good family and daughters of good family attain and abide in these four dharmas, they will not harm themselves."
What are these four?

First, not harboring a harmful mind toward sentient beings; second, not engaging in disputes or litigation with Dharma masters; third, though one’s own understanding may be slight, not disparaging others who possess broad and profound wisdom;
and fourth, thinking to oneself: "All these meanings were spoken by the Buddha; therefore, I should honor them, remaining humble, reverent, and compliant."
"These are the four dharmas by which one does not harm oneself.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

If there were a bodhisattva who, with the seven treasures filling as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, made offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—doing so every single day in this manner, offering such gifts to the Buddhas without ceasing.

If, moreover, one receives this essential sūtra of the Vaipulya teachings, transcribes it upon bamboo or silk, and proclaims it even once, the merit thereof shall surpass that of making offerings to all the Buddhas.
The reason for this is that the merits of giving, observing the precepts, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom are all unable to equal the wholesome karma of such a person.
The *Jifang* (Therapeutic Prescriptions) and other such studies are the essentials of the scriptures; yet the learning of a Bodhisattva is of peerless virtue, walking alone without equal.

While this sutra was being preached, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of thirty Ganges Rivers all attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance that phenomena are unarisen); Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of seventy Ganges Rivers all attained the stage of non-retrogression—destined to achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; and sixty billion *nayuta* hundreds of thousands of beings dwelling within this trichiliocosm, upon hearing this scripture, all together exhorted and assisted one another to resolve their minds toward the Way, and with a single mind they attained liberation, transcending the hardships of birth and death for eighty *kalpas*, and all simultaneously attained the stage of non-retrogression.
The Buddha spoke thus.

All those in the assembly—the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and the people of the world—hearing what the Buddha had said, were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
